content: The measurement of particulate matter (PM) exposure in young children has been a significant challenge, which explains the limited availability of such data in studies. Some studies have used simple diffusion tubes to measure carbon monoxide as a proxy for PM, but this approach is suboptimal. Conducting air quality measurements requires the use of standardized methods, with meticulous attention to equipment calibration and quality control/assurance. Personal exposure measurement is particularly critical for studies assessing health risks or directly linking exposure to health outcomes. Other sources of combustion, such as brick kilns, contribute to air pollution in both rural and urban areas, in addition to household fuel combustion. Since outdoor pollution can infiltrate homes, strategies for maintaining clean indoor air must be coordinated with policies aimed at controlling these additional sources. The measurement of ambient (outdoor) air quality is also a vital component of household air pollution (HAP) control strategies. In many rural and other settings where solid fuel use is prevalent, household fuel combustion is a major, if not the primary, source of pollution. Biomass (commonly in the form of charcoal or wood) and kerosene are still widely used for cooking and heating in urban and peri-urban areas, significantly contributing to ambient air pollution in cities where such practices are common. Therefore, it is essential to monitor and evaluate the contributions of household fuel combustion to ambient air pollution in urban areas and assess the use and impacts of clean fuels and energy technologies in these settings. The World Health Organization (WHO) air quality guidelines (AQGs) apply to pollutants in all settings and can serve as a foundation for regulation and policy to support the transition to low-emission household energy. The monitoring and evaluation (M&E) strategy should include methods to assess whether new technologies and fuels in everyday use are achieving the desired impact on critical health outcomes. Studies should ideally be conducted over several months of use, or preferably for more than one year. Levels of HAP and personal exposure, whether measured directly or estimated through modeling, are valuable indicators of risk. Demonstrating the health effects of large-scale programs is an essential component of the M&E strategy and related research efforts. However, given the resource and technical challenges involved, this may be best managed with contributions from international partners. Measuring the use, maintenance, and replacement of technology and fuel interventions, as well as understanding why households make different choices, is also important. Quantitative tools (e.g., stove-use monitors) and qualitative methods (e.g., in-depth interviews, focus group discussions) can provide a more comprehensive understanding of what is happening and why. WHO will collaborate with its partners, including the research community, to facilitate the development and application of improved M&E methods and related research on health risks and intervention impacts. The findings from these research and evaluation activities will be incorporated into the guidelines, updating them as necessary. Measuring the incidence of major child health outcomes, such as pneumonia, requires the application of well-standardized diagnostic methods, physician assessment, and potentially additional investigations such as X-rays and sample analyses to identify the causative organism (virus or bacteria). Spirometry, the measurement of lung function, is essential for diagnosing chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). This requires thorough staff training, careful explanation to the subjects being examined, and expert quality control. Finally, it is crucial to evaluate programs designed to address the adverse health and other impacts resulting from inefficient, polluting, and unsafe household energy. This evaluation should assess the program's organization (structure), processes, activities, and impacts, drawing on many of the components described above. Research priorities include studies on the use and impacts of improved household energy technologies and clean fuels under real-life conditions to better estimate the effectiveness of interventions for major causes of disease, including cardiovascular disease. These studies can also provide insights into the cost-effectiveness of home energy interventions compared to other preventive measures. Other relevant research questions include the role of black carbon, the impacts of kerosene, and factors influencing sustained adoption of clean energy solutions. WHO will work with its partners and the research community to ensure these research priorities are addressed, that high-quality and well-standardized methods are used, and that results are incorporated into policy in a timely manner.
